welcome_seq.preview: A quick note on who I am and why I'm in your inbox — plus one thing you can do today.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Dan here from Frayne Electrical.

You signed up, so I'll tell you what you're getting: short emails, plain English, nothing padded out.

I work mostly on older houses round Wakefield, Horbury and Ossett. 1930s and 1950s semis, mainly. The ones where the surveyor flagged the electrics as dated and the owners filed that warning away under 'sort it later.'

That's what these emails are about — not selling you something every other day, but giving you a straight read on what's worth worrying about, what can genuinely wait, and how to tell the difference.

The one useful thing for today: if you have a fuse board that still uses old-style rewirable fuses — the kind with thin wire threaded through a ceramic block — take a photo of it and send it to me. I'll tell you whether it needs replacing or whether it can sit a while longer. No obligation, no quote attached.

P.S. If at any point these emails aren't useful, unsubscribe at the bottom. No hard feelings.

subject_variants.subject: It's not really about the socket, is it
The smell you can't quite locate
What's actually keeping you up at 3am

welcome_seq.preview: The socket is the excuse to ring. This is what's really sitting underneath it.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Most people don't ring an electrician because they want an electrician.

They ring because there's a socket that's gone brown near a child's bedroom, or a faint smell of warm plastic they can't quite place, or lights that flicker and then don't — and they've been mentally cataloguing it for weeks, running through the house in their head at 3am before they can let themselves sleep.

The socket is just the thing that finally tips them into picking up the phone.

The real problem is the guilt that sits underneath it. Most older houses were bought with a survey that flagged the electrics as dated. Most people told themselves they'd deal with it. Then life happened, and later kept moving.

I see this in almost every house I walk into in Horbury or Wakefield or Dewsbury. The wiring issue is real. But the thing the person at the door actually needs is someone to walk them through what's there — clearly, in writing — and tell them the truth about how serious it is.

That's most of the job, honestly. The physical work comes second.

Tomorrow I'll tell you what makes the difference between a straight answer and one that's just bigger than it needs to be.
welcome_seq.cta: Reply and tell me — how long has whatever you're noticing been there? I read every reply.

subject_variants.subject: Why I write down what can wait
The part of the report nobody else puts in writing
How to spot a quote you can actually trust

welcome_seq.preview: There's one thing I do on every job that seems to surprise people. It probably shouldn't.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Here's something that shouldn't be unusual but apparently is.

When I inspect a house, I photograph everything. Then I write up the findings in plain English — what's dangerous, what's wrong, and what can honestly wait a few years.

That last part is the one that surprises people.

Most reports tell you what needs doing. They don't tell you what can sit. That matters, because if you don't know what can wait, you have no way to judge whether a quote is honest or just large.

I put it in writing because a fixed price is only worth something if the scope behind it is clear. If I say the job is £X and the report names exactly what that covers — and what it doesn't cover because it doesn't need covering yet — then you can hold me to it. That's the deal.

I also turn up when I said I would. I know that shouldn't be a selling point in this trade, but apparently it is.

No vague arrival windows. Booked is booked.

None of this is complicated. It's just what the job looks like when it's done right.
welcome_seq.cta: Reply if you've got a question about what a proper electrical inspection covers — happy to answer.

What happened when we opened up the old wiring

welcome_seq.preview: I'll let the people I've worked for say this one. Their words, not mine.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

I don't normally lead with what customers say, but this one is worth reading in full.

"Dan found live wires behind our bathroom wall that the last electrician had just plastered over. I honestly felt sick. He stayed till gone 9 making it safe and never charged a penny extra. First night in months I haven't laid there smelling imaginary burning."

That's a real message. Not a stat, not a case study dressed up — someone's actual words after the job was done.

The live wires behind the wall are more common than people think in older houses. Someone's had a go at something, it's gone wrong, and the quickest fix has been to cover it over and hope. That doesn't make it safe. It makes it someone else's problem until it isn't.

When I find something like that I document it, explain it in plain English on the spot, and sort it before I leave. The fixed price stays the same.

Another one, from a different job:

"Thought a full rewire meant living on a building site for a month. Done in six days and they hoovered up better than my cleaner does. Mum's booked in for hers next."

The mess and disruption worry is the one I hear most often. I'll address that directly in tomorrow's email.

subject_variants.subject: How to check your fuse board yourself in five minutes
Three things in older houses that are worth checking today
What to look for before you ring anyone

welcome_seq.preview: A few things you can check yourself right now — no tools, no qualifications needed.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

You don't need me to tell you whether some things are worth acting on. Here are three you can check yourself.

One: Open your fuse board and look at what's inside. If you see old ceramic fuses with thin wire threaded through them rather than modern circuit breakers, that fuse board is overdue. It won't trip properly in a fault — it'll let the current keep running. That matters on older wiring.

Two: Look at the sockets in any room where you can smell warm plastic or where you've had a flickering light. Discolouration — brown, scorched, yellowed around the face — means heat has been building somewhere behind the wall. That is not a cosmetic issue.

Three: Think about the date you moved in. If the wiring has never been inspected in writing since you bought the house, you don't actually know what's in the walls. A survey warning is not an inspection. It's a flag that someone else should look.

None of those checks take more than five minutes. What you do with what you find is a different question.

If any of the three applies to your house, the honest next step is a certified inspection — photographs, plain English report, fixed price, in writing.

That's exactly what the Home Safety Check from Frayne Electrical is. I'll tell you more about it tomorrow.
welcome_seq.cta: Reply with what you found — even just describing it — and I'll tell you how urgent it looks.

welcome_seq.preview: The hesitations people have before booking — I'd rather deal with them directly than leave them sitting there.
welcome_seq.body:
Hi {{first_name}},

Three things come up in almost every first conversation. I'd rather deal with them directly.

First: Is the scope genuine or inflated? This is the one people don't always say out loud but are absolutely thinking. My answer is the written report. When I name what can honestly wait — as a line item, in plain English — you can see what I'm not billing for. That's the check. No written scope means no accountability.

Second: Will the house be a building site for weeks? A full rewire in a standard semi takes around six days. We work room by room, we protect what we can, and we clean up properly each day. One customer put it plainly: they said their mum booked hers after seeing the result. That's not a selling line — it's just what a tidy finish looks like.

Third: There is always someone cheaper. Yes. There is also always someone who quotes on a fuse board without visiting the house, gives you a low number, and then finds reasons for extras once the ceiling is open. A fixed price agreed in writing after Dan has actually seen the job is a different thing from a quote over the phone. It is not the same product at a higher price.

If you have a different worry I haven't covered, reply and ask. Straightforward questions get straightforward answers.

And then there's the one nobody really talks about: the running mental overhead. The socket you're half-watching. The smell you keep telling yourself is probably nothing. The habit of going round before bed checking what's switched off.
